searchText: <@273808422753796097> Why do you think consensus layer checksums are bad? I can see a mild argument for them not adding enough value to be worth it, but not an argument for "bad". Unless perhaps you mean "not worth the reduction in number of bits of security"? add no value relative to non-consensus-layer checksums, and increase consensus-layer complexity and yes, they do reduce bits of security too The value consensus-layer-checksums add is they force consistency across implementations, it's a developer experience and user experience issue masquerading as a safety issue. So I don't even expect people to be passing around validator withdrawal keys the way we pass around addresses and validators already have IDs that they can be referred to by, from which a node can extract the withdrawal commitment I misread (or didn't read enough scrollback) and thought the discussion was the pubkeys... oops. hmm..... what is a usecase for passing even pubkeys around? just pubkeys in general... In general, I feel like we should just standardize on a "display format" that includes checksums and then we can later decide what gets displayed through the display format The problem is people can still screw that up. This could even just be mixed case hex, though the problem with mixed case hex that we've seen is that mixed case hex is too easy to be "too lenient" for accidentally, because you support it without trying So if we adopt any of the base 32's Then if most clients support it network effect would force all of them to Some variant of bech32 seems like a decent enough option if made against a 32-byte value (which would be hash of pubkey with version and shard ID replacing some bytes). bech32 itself got a bit mixed up with the segwit stuff being part of the spec, if I remember correctly From https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/issues/1183 a bech32 encoding of a 32-byte value would look something like `eth1m0ad9f4lkrnlru8523sfgnaa3ha87d76q6jdzwees0xfpw6xjcas7ucq5e`, which is large but not egregiously so
